judges.name: Kansas R. Gooden
judges.ballot_question: Shall Judge Kansas R. Gooden of the Third District Court of Appeal be retained in office?
judges.background: Kansas R. Gooden holds a bachelor's degree from James Madison University and a law degree from St. Thomas University. Before joining the bench she spent about 16 years in private practice, most recently as a shareholder and appellate practice group leader at the firm Boyd & Jenerette, where she was board certified in appellate practice and handled more than 400 civil appeals. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Third District Court of Appeal on June 28, 2024, to fill the seat left vacant by the death of Judge Eric Hendon. This is her first merit-retention election; judges appointed to a district court of appeal must stand for retention at the next general election held more than one year after taking office.

rulings.case: Contragolpe LLC v. 505 NE 30 Street, LLC (No. 3D23-1487)
rulings.what_it_decided: A three-judge panel reversed a Miami-Dade trial court's summary judgment, holding that the contract language was ambiguous and the trial judge should not have resolved that ambiguity by weighing conflicting outside evidence at the summary-judgment stage. The case was sent back for further proceedings.

rulings.what_it_decided: The panel affirmed a Miami-Dade trial court ruling for the homeowner in a property-insurance dispute in a short unsigned (per curiam) opinion that cited an earlier Third DCA decision, Citizens Property Insurance Corp. v. Laguerre (2018).

rulings.what_it_decided: The panel reversed a trial court decision and sent the case back in a dispute over deposits owed to condominium purchasers, relying on the court's earlier ruling in the same litigation that the developer's construction delay did not breach the purchase agreements.

judges.record_summary: No opinion authored by Judge Gooden could be located through search snippets; the rulings listed above are cases where published panel listings show she joined the decision. In Wright-Johnson v. State (No. 3D23-1452, 2025) the Justia listing shows her as concurring in the result only, but the snippet did not describe the ruling. In the Miami-Dade County Bar Association's 2026 judicial poll (631 respondents, closed July 3, 2026), 232 lawyers said she should be retained, 91 said no and 247 had no opinion, about 71.8% 'yes' among those expressing a view. The Federalist Society lists her as a contributor on its website. No organized retention campaign for or against her was found.

judges.name: Monica Gordo
judges.ballot_question: Shall Judge Monica Gordo of the Third District Court of Appeal be retained in office?
judges.background: Monica Gordo earned both her bachelor's degree and her law degree from the University of Miami and was admitted to the Florida Bar in 1999. She worked for more than 11 years as an assistant state attorney in Miami-Dade, where she became a division chief supervising a felony division. She was elected to the Eleventh Judicial Circuit (Miami-Dade) in 2010, was sworn in in January 2011 and served about eight years in the criminal, civil and family divisions. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Third District Court of Appeal on April 25, 2019, to fill the vacancy created when Barbara Lagoa was elevated to the Florida Supreme Court. Voters retained her on Nov. 3, 2020, with about 73.8% voting yes.

judges.name: Fleur Jeannine Lobree
judges.ballot_question: Shall Judge Fleur Jeannine Lobree of the Third District Court of Appeal be retained in office?
judges.background: Fleur Jeannine Lobree earned her bachelor's degree from Florida State University and her law degree from the University of Miami. Her earlier career included work as an assistant state attorney in Miami-Dade, an assistant attorney general, a law clerk to Third DCA Judge Rodolfo Sorondo Jr., and an associate at the law firm Hicks, Anderson & Kneale. She served as a Miami-Dade County Court judge from 2011 to 2013 and, after appointment by Gov. Rick Scott, as an Eleventh Judicial Circuit judge from 2013 to 2015, then returned to the State Attorney's Office. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Third District Court of Appeal on April 25, 2019, to fill the vacancy created when Robert Luck was elevated to the Florida Supreme Court. Voters retained her on Nov. 3, 2020, with about 72.8% voting yes.

judges.name: Thomas Logue
judges.ballot_question: Shall Judge Thomas Logue of the Third District Court of Appeal be retained in office?
judges.background: Thomas W. Logue earned his undergraduate degree from Dickinson College and his law degree from Duke University, where he served on the editorial board of the Duke Law Journal. Before joining the bench he spent about 30 years as an assistant county attorney for Miami-Dade County, litigating cases and arguing appeals in state and federal courts and advising the county commission and property appraiser. Gov. Rick Scott appointed him to the Third District Court of Appeal in 2012 (Ballotpedia lists his start date as June 7, 2012; the Florida Bar's appellate section newsletter reports the appointment as July 6, 2012). He has served as the court's chief judge; 2025 opinions list him as 'Logue, C.J.' He was retained by voters on Nov. 3, 2020, and has taught at the Florida Judicial College.

rulings.case: City of Aventura v. Jimenez
rulings.what_it_decided: The court reversed the dismissal of a red-light camera ticket issued by a private vendor on Aventura's behalf. Judge Logue wrote that the vendor's role in sorting camera images was essentially clerical and that a police officer must still make a real review before a citation issues. The ruling disagreed with a Fourth District decision striking down Hollywood's program, and the court certified questions to the Florida Supreme Court.

rulings.case: McGillis v. Department of Economic Opportunity (No. 3D15-2758)
rulings.what_it_decided: The court held that a former Uber driver was an independent contractor, not an employee, for purposes of state reemployment-assistance (unemployment) benefits. Judge Logue wrote that the key factor is how much control the company has over the work, and that drivers decide whether, when, where and how to give rides, which does not fit the control an employer has over a traditional employee.
rulings.note: The ruling addressed only unemployment benefits, not employment status for all purposes.

judges.record_summary: In the Florida Bar's 2020 statewide merit-retention poll, 83% of responding lawyers recommended retaining Judge Miller, and voters retained her that year with about 75% (Ballotpedia). In October 2025 the Florida Judicial Qualifications Commission (JQC) filed formal charges against her over text messages she exchanged with Miami-Dade State Attorney Katherine Fernandez Rundle; according to the ABA Journal and Florida Bulldog, the JQC alleged the texts sought to influence how the State Attorney's Office handled a post-conviction resentencing case in which Miller was a victim and witness, and the charges cite Canons 1, 2A, 3B(9) and 5A of the Florida Code of Judicial Conduct. Her attorney, Warren Lindsey, filed a motion to dismiss in April 2026 arguing the texts are speech protected by the First Amendment and that she was acting as a crime victim and fact witness; the JQC hearing panel chaired by Judge Morris Silberman said it would rule in writing. No ruling on the motion, and no Florida Supreme Court decision (which would make any final determination on discipline), was found in search results as of late October 2026. A column on SocialMiami.com argued she was unfairly accused. In the Miami-Dade County Bar Association's 2026 judicial poll (631 respondents, closed July 3, 2026), 314 lawyers said she should be retained, 172 said no and 91 had no opinion, about 64.6% 'yes' among those expressing a view, the lowest of the five Third DCA judges on the 2026 ballot. No organized retention campaign for or against her was found.
